claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by formation of a chromium-rich oxide layer.
The protective chromium-rich oxide layer is continuous.
The protective chromium-rich oxide layer is adherent.
The chromium-rich oxide layer is self-healing after minor damage.
The chromium-rich oxide layer limits corrosion by acting as a barrier to aggressive species.
The steels can begin with a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements, including chromium.
The specimens can begin with an unoxidized, defect-minimized surface.
The relevant structural mediator is a chromium-rich Cr2O3 surface layer.
Chromium preferentially oxidizes during corrosive exposure.
Preferential chromium oxidation produces a thin, protective Cr2O3 layer.
Available chromium rapidly reforms the oxide after minor film damage.
Reformation of the chromium oxide barrier prevents further metal dissolution.
Steels with higher chromium content should form thicker chromium oxide layers than lower-chromium steels under identical conditions.
Steels with higher chromium content should form more uniform chromium oxide layers than lower-chromium steels.
Steels with higher chromium content should show greater passive-film self-healing than lower-chromium steels.
Steels with higher chromium content should have significantly lower weight-loss, pitting, and electrochemically measured corrosion rates than lower-chromium steels.
The proposed mechanism should operate at moderate temperatures in acidic or chloride-containing solutions when oxygen is available.
The proposed mechanism may fail when passive-film formation is chemically destabilized or conditions are far outside the tested ranges.
